replacement: That, or something like it, was the speech of Phaedrus. Some other speeches followed which Aristodemus did not remember, and the next one he repeated was that of Pausanias. Phaedrus, he said, I do not think the subject has been set before us in quite the right form. We should not be called on to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be well enough. But since there is more than one Love, you should have begun by deciding which of them we were to praise. I will correct this fault. First I will tell you which Love deserves praise, and then I will try to praise that one in a manner worthy of him. We all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love. But since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder has no mother and is called the heavenly Aphrodite, the daughter of Uranus. The younger is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, and we call her the common Aphrodite. The Love who works with her is rightly called common, just as the other is called heavenly. All the gods ought to be praised, but not without distinguishing their natures, so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now actions differ according to the way they are performed.
